summary: For ages 7–9: lightning is a giant electrical spark that forms in storm clouds, thunder is the sound that spark makes, and both happen at essentially the same instant — we see the flash before we hear the boom because light travels far faster than sound. The memorable, measurable core is the flash-then-boom delay: counting the seconds after the flash estimates how far away the storm is (sound travels roughly 1 km in about 3 seconds). A shrinking gap means the storm is getting closer. Keep charge separation qualitative (charge builds up, then jumps as a spark), and address fears directly: thunder is only a sound and cannot hurt you; respect the lightning.
misconceptions: Thunder and lightning are separate events — thunder is the SOUND made by the lightning
Lightning comes before thunder in time — they happen together; we just SEE the flash before the sound arrives
Thunder can hurt you — it is only a sound; the danger is the lightning
Bigger/louder thunder means the lightning is more dangerous — loudness mainly reflects how close it is
Light and sound travel at the same speed

activities.title: Count the storm's distance
steps: Watch or imagine a distant flash light up the sky, then count the seconds — one, two, three — until the boom arrives.
Use the rule that sound travels roughly 1 km in about 3 seconds to turn the counted gap into an approximate distance.
Imagine (or explore with a simulation) moving the storm closer and farther: note how the gap between flash and boom shrinks toward zero as it nears and stretches out as it recedes.
State in your own words why the flash arrives first: light is near-instant, sound crawls, so the silence after the flash is literally measuring the distance.
activities.insight: Light and sound leave the lightning at the same instant, but light arrives almost immediately while sound takes a few seconds; the flash-to-boom gap is therefore a ruler for how far away the storm is, and a shrinking gap means it is coming closer.

activities.title: Optional interactive timing: tap the flash, tap the boom
steps: In a simulation, tap when the flash appears and tap again when the boom arrives; let the tool time the gap and convert it to a distance.
Drag a storm-distance slider toward you and watch the gap shrink toward zero (flash and boom arriving almost together right overhead), then drag it away and watch the delay stretch out.
Optionally turn on a 'count with me' overlay that models the seconds-to-distance rule as you count.
activities.insight: Directly manipulating the storm's distance and watching the measured gap respond is intended to link the abstract speed difference to a felt, continuous relationship between delay and distance.

activities.title: Name the parts of a storm cloud (supporting scaffold)
steps: Look at a storm-cloud diagram and identify where charge builds up, where the spark jumps, and where the boom comes from.
Explain in a sentence that charge builds in the cloud and then jumps as a spark (the lightning), and the sound of that spark is the thunder.
activities.insight: Lightning is an electrical discharge — charge builds and then jumps as a spark — and thunder is the sound that spark makes; this is kept qualitative with no circuit detail.

activities.title: Storm safety and facing the fear
steps: Decide, from whether the flash-to-boom gap is shrinking or growing, whether a storm is coming closer or moving away, and remember that if you can hear thunder at all you should already be indoors, whatever the gap.
Discuss what actually makes the thunder sound, and explain why thunder itself cannot hurt you while lightning is the thing to respect.
Talk through age-appropriate storm-safety rules (e.g. when thunder roars, go indoors, even if the flash-to-boom gap is long).
activities.insight: Loudness of thunder mainly reflects how close the lightning is, not how dangerous the sound is. If you can hear thunder at all, lightning is close enough to be a danger, so go indoors. The gap tells you roughly how far away the storm is and whether it is coming closer, and it is the lightning, not the sound, that poses the danger.

checkQuestion: In a storm you see the lightning flash, then a few seconds later you hear the thunder. Do the flash and the thunder happen at the same time or at different times? And why do you see the flash before you hear the bang?
checkAnswer: They happen at essentially the same instant — the lightning heats the air so fast it explodes outward and that IS the thunder. You see the flash first because light travels vastly faster than sound, so the bang takes a few seconds to reach your ears. Counting the gap tells you roughly how far away the strike is.
